concepts.title: Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and Running Totals
concepts.description: Window functions compute a value across a set of related rows (a rank, a running total, a moving average) without collapsing those rows into one summary row the way GROUP BY does, letting you keep row-level detail and aggregate context in the same result set.
learningObjectives: Explain what a window function is and how OVER() differs fundamentally from GROUP BY -- rows are preserved, not collapsed into one row per group.
Use ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() correctly, and explain how each behaves differently when there are ties.
Use PARTITION BY to reset a window calculation per group without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY would.
Compute a running total and a moving average using SUM() OVER and AVG() OVER with an explicit frame clause.
Explain the default frame boundary Postgres applies when ORDER BY is present inside OVER() versus when it's absent, and why that default causes a common bug.

sections.heading: Window Functions vs GROUP BY: Rows Survive
sections.body:
GROUP BY answers 'give me one row per group.' A window function answers a different question: 'for each row, compute something using a window of other rows around it, but keep every original row in the output.' The `OVER()` clause is what turns an ordinary aggregate-looking function into a window function: adding `OVER (...)` after `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(...)`, or `AVG(...)` tells Postgres not to collapse rows, but instead to compute that aggregate across a defined set of rows (the 'window') *for each row individually*, attaching the result as an extra column.

```sql
-- GROUP BY: one row per customer, order-level detail is gone
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- Window function: every order row survives, PLUS the customer's total
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders;
```

The second query returns as many rows as `orders` has, and each row also carries `customer_total`, computed across all of that customer's orders. GROUP BY alone can't give you the detail and the aggregate on the same row; you would need a self-join or a subquery to reattach the aggregate to each detail row.

sections.heading: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK: Ranking With and Without Gaps
sections.body:
These three functions all assign an integer to each row based on its position in an order, but they disagree about what happens when two rows tie on the ordering expression.

```sql
-- scores: (Amy, 95), (Ben, 90), (Cara, 90), (Dan, 85)
SELECT name, score,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM scores;

-- name | score | row_num | rank | dense_rank
-- Amy  |  95   |    1    |  1   |     1
-- Ben  |  90   |    2    |  2   |     2
-- Cara |  90   |    3    |  2   |     2
-- Dan  |  85   |    4    |  4   |     3
```

`ROW_NUMBER()` assigns a strictly increasing integer with no regard for ties. Ben and Cara tied at 90, but ROW_NUMBER arbitrarily breaks the tie and gives them 2 and 3 (which one gets which is not deterministic unless you add a tiebreaker column to ORDER BY). `RANK()` gives tied rows the *same* rank (both Ben and Cara get 2), but then leaves a gap afterward: Dan, the next distinct value, jumps to 4 because two rows already occupied rank 2. `DENSE_RANK()` also gives tied rows the same rank, but never leaves a gap: Dan gets 3 because dense ranking counts *distinct* values seen so far, not row positions. Give each of these an `ORDER BY` inside the `OVER()` clause. Without one PostgreSQL raises no error, but every row is a peer of every other, so `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` return 1 for all of them and `ROW_NUMBER()` numbers rows in arbitrary order. NULLs sort last under `ORDER BY ... ASC` and first under `DESC` in Postgres, so a NULL score would take rank 1 in the query above; add `NULLS LAST` if missing values should not win.

sections.heading: PARTITION BY: Resetting the Window Per Group
sections.body:
`PARTITION BY` inside `OVER()` is what makes a window calculation restart independently for each group, conceptually similar to what GROUP BY does for aggregation, but without collapsing the rows in that group down to one. You can think of it as 'apply this window function separately within each partition, as if the other partitions didn't exist.'

```sql
-- Rank employees by salary, separately within each department
SELECT name, department, salary,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees;
```

Without `PARTITION BY department`, `RANK()` would rank every employee against the entire company, competing across departments that have nothing to do with each other. With it, the ranking resets to 1 for every department. Rows whose partition column is NULL are grouped together into one partition of their own. `PARTITION BY` can take multiple columns, like GROUP BY, and it combines freely with `ORDER BY` inside the same `OVER()` clause: the partition determines *which* rows the window function considers together; the order (where relevant, as for ranking or running totals) determines the sequence it processes them in *within* that partition.

sections.heading: Running Totals and Frame Clauses: the Default Frame
sections.body:
A running total asks 'for each row, sum every row up to and including this one, in some order.' The **frame clause** defines 'up to and including this one', and its default surprises most people the first time they hit it.

```sql
SELECT order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM daily_sales;
```

This produces a running total because of a default frame you didn't write: whenever `ORDER BY` is present inside `OVER()` and no frame clause is given, Postgres defaults to `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, meaning 'everything from the start of the partition up through the current row and any peers tied with it on the ORDER BY expression.' The peers matter: if two rows share an `order_date`, both show the total *including both amounts*. Write `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (plus a tiebreaker) if you want the total to advance row by row. The earlier `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)` had *no* `ORDER BY`, so every row in the partition was a peer and it computed each customer's grand total. **Adding an ORDER BY to a window function that had none changes its default frame**, so a small edit can turn a full-partition SUM into a running total.

Here is the peer effect with a tie. Take `daily_sales` rows `(01-01, 100)`, `(01-02, 150)`, `(01-02, 50)`, `(01-03, 80)`. The default frame gives running totals of 100, 300, 300, 380: both 01-02 rows show 300, because each one includes its peer. With `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` you get 100, 250, 300, 380, but which of the two 01-02 rows shows 250 is arbitrary until you add a tiebreaker to the window's ORDER BY.

The same default frame explains a classic surprise with `LAST_VALUE`. `LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)` does not return the last amount in the partition. The frame ends at the current row (or its last peer), so it just echoes the current row's value. Write `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` to reach the true last row.

For a moving average over a fixed-size trailing window rather than everything-so-far, specify the frame with `ROWS BETWEEN`:

```sql
SELECT order_date, amount,
       AVG(amount) OVER (
           ORDER BY order_date
           ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS moving_avg_3day
FROM daily_sales;
```

This averages only the current row and the two immediately preceding it. It counts rows, not days: if a date is missing from `daily_sales`, the window reaches further back than three days. For calendar days use `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '2 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes: Filtering on a Window Function, and Picking the Right Ranking Function
sections.body:
You cannot filter on a window function's result using `WHERE` in the same `SELECT` that computes it: `SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rn FROM orders WHERE rn = 1` fails because `WHERE` is evaluated before the SELECT list's expressions (including window functions) are computed, so `rn` doesn't exist yet. PostgreSQL has no 'HAVING for window functions' (some databases add `QUALIFY` for this); the standard fix is to compute the window function in a subquery or CTE, then filter on it in an outer query where it exists as a column:

```sql
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1;   -- most recent order per customer
```

The other frequent mistake is reaching for the wrong ranking function for a 'top N per group' query. If ties should count as occupying the same rank and you want gaps afterward (competition-style ranking, like 'tied for 2nd place, so no one is 3rd'), use `RANK()`. If ties should count as the same rank with no gap (dense, sequential placement bands), use `DENSE_RANK()`. If you want one winner per group, such as 'the most recent order per customer' even when two orders share a timestamp, use `ROW_NUMBER()`, and add enough columns to `ORDER BY` (like a tiebreaking `id`) to make the choice reproducible.

The same choice applies to 'top 3 per group'. `rn <= 3` with `ROW_NUMBER()` returns exactly three rows per group, while `rank <= 3` can return more than three when ties straddle the cutoff. That is sometimes what you want and sometimes a surprise in a report with a fixed number of slots.

examples.title: Running Total of Daily Sales
examples.code:
-- daily_sales: (2026-01-01, 100), (2026-01-02, 150), (2026-01-03, 80)

SELECT order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM daily_sales
ORDER BY order_date;

-- order_date | amount | running_total
-- 2026-01-01 |  100   |     100
-- 2026-01-02 |  150   |     250
-- 2026-01-03 |   80   |     330
examples.explanation: Each row's `running_total` sums every row's `amount` from the start of the ordering through the current row, thanks to the default frame (`RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`) that Postgres applies automatically whenever `ORDER BY` appears inside `OVER()` with no frame clause. Notice the query's own `ORDER BY order_date` at the very end is separate from the `ORDER BY` inside `OVER(...)`: the outer one controls what order the final result set is displayed in; the inner one controls what order the window function processes rows in to compute the running total. They happen to match here, but they don't have to: you could order the *output* by amount descending while the running total was still computed in date order internally.

examples.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK Side by Side With a Tie
examples.code:
-- scores: (Amy, 95), (Ben, 90), (Cara, 90), (Dan, 85)

SELECT name, score,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM scores
ORDER BY score DESC;

-- name | score | row_num | rank | dense_rank
-- Amy  |  95   |    1    |  1   |     1
-- Ben  |  90   |    2    |  2   |     2
-- Cara |  90   |    3    |  2   |     2
-- Dan  |  85   |    4    |  4   |     3
examples.explanation: Ben and Cara are tied at 90. ROW_NUMBER ignores the tie completely and hands out 2 and 3 in whatever order it encounters the tied rows. Which one gets 2 and which gets 3 is not guaranteed unless a tiebreaker column is added to ORDER BY. RANK gives both of them 2 (correctly reflecting that they're tied), but then Dan's rank jumps straight to 4, leaving 3 unused, because two rows already claimed rank 2. DENSE_RANK also gives both of them 2, but Dan gets 3 because dense ranking counts distinct score values seen so far (95, then 90, then 85 is the third distinct value) rather than row positions.

examples.title: Top N Per Group: Most Recent Order Per Customer
examples.code:
-- This does NOT work: rn doesn't exist yet when WHERE runs.
SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
FROM orders
WHERE rn = 1;
-- ERROR:  column "rn" does not exist

-- Correct: compute the window function in a subquery, filter in the outer query.
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
examples.explanation: The broken version tries to filter on `rn` in the same SELECT that defines it, but WHERE is evaluated first. The fix wraps the window function in a subquery (or a CTE), so that the outer WHERE sees `rn` as an ordinary column. PostgreSQL 15 and later even recognize `rn = 1` here and stop numbering each partition early. `PARTITION BY customer_id` resets the numbering to 1 for every customer, and `ORDER BY order_date DESC` means rn = 1 is each customer's most recent order. GROUP BY with `MAX(order_date)` would give you the date but not that row's `order_id` and `amount`. Change the filter to `rn <= 3` and you get each customer's three most recent orders, the usual form of this pattern.

misconceptions.description: A window function with PARTITION BY works like GROUP BY -- it collapses all the rows in each partition down into one summary row.
misconceptions.clarification: PARTITION BY only determines which rows a window function considers together when computing its result for each row; it does not remove or merge any rows. Every row is still in the output with an extra computed column. GROUP BY reduces N rows to however many distinct groups exist; a window function with PARTITION BY still returns N rows. The row count is the quick check: adding `SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` to a query never changes how many rows it returns.
misconceptions.fact: PARTITION BY only determines which rows a window function considers together when computing its result for each row; it does not remove or merge any rows.

misconceptions.description: You can filter on a window function's result directly in the WHERE clause of the same SELECT that computes it, the same way you'd filter on any other computed column.
misconceptions.clarification: WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list (including any window functions in it) is computed, following the same logical order-of-operations that makes HAVING (not WHERE) the clause required for filtering on aggregates. Referencing the alias in WHERE raises 'column does not exist', and writing the window function itself in WHERE raises 'window functions are not allowed in WHERE'. Compute it in a subquery or CTE and filter on it from the outer query.
misconceptions.fact: WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list (including any window functions in it) is computed, following the same logical order-of-operations that makes HAVING (not WHERE) the clause required for filtering on aggregates.

exercises.prompt: Given `results: (Amy, 100), (Ben, 100), (Cara, 95), (Dan, 90)`, what does each of the three ranking columns show for Dan?
exercises.code:
SELECT name, points,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM results
ORDER BY points DESC;
hints: Amy and Ben are tied for first at 100 points. Work out what each of the three functions assigns to them before worrying about Dan or Cara.
RANK() leaves a gap in the numbering equal to the number of rows tied ahead of the current one; DENSE_RANK() never leaves gaps.
Cara is the third-ranked person by row position, but the second DISTINCT score value (100, then 95). Dan is the fourth by position but the third distinct value.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Dan's row_num is 4, rank is 4, and dense_rank is 3. Amy and Ben tie at 100 (row_num 1 and 2 in some order, rank 1 for both, dense_rank 1 for both). Cara at 95 gets row_num 3, rank 3, dense_rank 2. Dan at 90 gets row_num 4, rank 4 (no gap needed since Cara didn't tie with anyone), dense_rank 3 (the third distinct score value: 100, 95, 90).
exercises.solutionExplanation: ROW_NUMBER assigns strictly sequential integers regardless of ties, so by the time it reaches Dan (fourth row by position), it assigns 4. RANK gives Amy and Ben both rank 1 (tied for first), then Cara, having no one tied with her, gets rank 3. Rank 2 is skipped because two rows already occupied rank 1. Dan then gets rank 4, following on from Cara's 3 with no further gap since Cara wasn't tied with anyone. DENSE_RANK counts distinct values only: 100 is the first distinct value (rank 1, shared by Amy and Ben), 95 is the second distinct value (Cara gets 2), and 90 is the third distinct value, so Dan gets dense_rank 3, one less than his RANK.

exercises.prompt: This query is meant to show only the highest-paid employee in each department, but it fails to run at all. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
SELECT name, department, salary,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees
WHERE dept_rank = 1;
hints: Think about the logical order a SELECT query executes in. Is a window function's result available yet by the time WHERE runs?
This is the same underlying issue as trying to filter on COUNT(*) in WHERE instead of HAVING, except PostgreSQL has no HAVING-equivalent clause for window functions.
Wrap the window function computation in a subquery (or a CTE), then filter on the dept_rank column from an outer query.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT name, department, salary, dept_rank
FROM (
    SELECT name, department, salary,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
    FROM employees
) ranked
WHERE dept_rank = 1;
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original query tries to filter on `dept_rank` in the very same SELECT that defines it, but WHERE is evaluated before window functions in the SELECT list are computed, so Postgres raises a 'column does not exist' error. With the window function in a subquery, `dept_rank` is an ordinary column to the outer query, no different from `salary` or `name`. The choice of RANK() over ROW_NUMBER() matters too: if two employees in a department tie for the highest salary, RANK() keeps both, whereas ROW_NUMBER() would arbitrarily keep one. If you need exactly one row per department even when salaries tie, use ROW_NUMBER() and add a unique column such as `id` to the ORDER BY so the choice is reproducible.

assessments.prompt: A developer writes `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)` (no ORDER BY inside OVER) expecting a running total per customer, but every row for a given customer shows the same total: their full sum, not a running total. What's happening?
options: PARTITION BY without ORDER BY is a syntax error that Postgres silently ignores by falling back to a full-table sum.
SUM() OVER() is broken for running totals and only AVG() OVER() can compute them.
The query needs GROUP BY added alongside PARTITION BY to compute a running total correctly.
Without an ORDER BY inside OVER(), the default frame is the entire partition.
assessments.explanation: Postgres's default frame depends on whether ORDER BY appears inside OVER(). With no ORDER BY, the frame covers the whole partition, so every row shows the customer's grand total. Adding ORDER BY inside OVER() changes the default frame to 'from the start of the partition through the current row,' which is what a running total needs. The “SUM() OVER() is broken for running totals…” option is false -- SUM() OVER() computes running totals correctly once ordered; the “PARTITION BY without ORDER BY…” option invents a nonexistent error/fallback; the “The query needs GROUP BY added alongside…” option is wrong because GROUP BY would collapse the rows a running total needs.

assessments.prompt: Explain how window functions differ from GROUP BY at a fundamental level, and use a running-total example to explain why the presence or absence of ORDER BY inside OVER() changes the result so dramatically.
assessments.modelAnswer: GROUP BY and window functions both let you compute an aggregate like SUM or COUNT across a set of related rows, but they differ in what happens to the original rows afterward. GROUP BY collapses every row in a group into one summary row per distinct group value, and the row-level detail is gone. A window function keeps every source row and gives each one an extra column holding the computed value. So it can answer questions GROUP BY alone cannot, like 'show me each order's amount alongside that customer's running total of all orders so far', which needs every order row in the output. The ORDER BY inside OVER() affects the default 'frame', the set of rows that contribute to a given row's aggregate. With no ORDER BY inside OVER(), the default frame is the entire partition (or the entire result set, if there's no PARTITION BY either), so every row in that partition gets the same value: the full sum. Once you add ORDER BY inside OVER(), the default frame changes to 'from the start of the partition through the current row' (plus any rows tied with it), so the aggregate accumulates as you move through the order: a running total. The danger is that adding or removing an ORDER BY in an existing OVER() clause turns one into the other with no error or warning. Rows with equal ORDER BY values are peers and share one running-total value under the default RANGE frame, which `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` avoids.

assessments.prompt: A query uses `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)` with no ORDER BY inside OVER(). Compared to a GROUP BY query computing the same per-customer sum, what's different about the number of rows each returns?
options: The window function query returns one row per original order row (nothing collapsed), with the customer's total attached as an extra column on every one of that customer's rows; the GROUP BY query collapses all of a customer's orders down into a single summary row.
The window function query returns fewer rows than the source table but more rows than the GROUP BY version.
GROUP BY preserves every original row, while PARTITION BY collapses rows down to one per customer.
Both return exactly one row per customer_id -- PARTITION BY is simply alternative syntax for GROUP BY.
assessments.explanation: PARTITION BY only determines which rows a window function considers together; every order row survives and gains a customer_total column. GROUP BY reduces the row count to one row per distinct customer_id, discarding individual order-level detail. The “Both return exactly one row per customer_id…” option treats them as interchangeable, but swapping one for the other changes the row count. The “The window function query returns fewer rows…” option invents an in-between row count that doesn't correspond to how either construct behaves. The “GROUP BY preserves every original row, while…” option reverses which construct does which.

assessments.prompt: Two rows tie on the value used in `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)`. What can you say about which of the two tied rows receives the lower number?
options: ROW_NUMBER() always assigns the lower number to whichever row was physically inserted into the table first.
PostgreSQL raises an error whenever ROW_NUMBER() encounters a tie, since ties are considered undefined input for this function.
Which tied row gets which number is not guaranteed to be deterministic or reproducible across runs unless an additional tiebreaker column is added to the ORDER BY.
ROW_NUMBER() automatically detects the tie and falls back to RANK()'s behavior, assigning both rows the same number.
assessments.explanation: ROW_NUMBER() ignores ties and hands out the next integer to each row in whatever order the database encounters them, which is not guaranteed to be stable or reproducible run to run unless the ORDER BY includes enough columns to fully distinguish every row (a tiebreaker like a unique id). The “ROW_NUMBER() always assigns the lower number…” option invents a rule about insertion order that PostgreSQL does not make. The “ROW_NUMBER() automatically detects the tie and falls…” option describes RANK()'s tie behavior; ROW_NUMBER() never gives two rows in a partition the same number. The “PostgreSQL raises an error whenever ROW_NUMBER() encounters…” option is false; ties are valid input and get an arbitrary assignment.

assessments.prompt: `AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` computes a moving average. For the 5th row in the ORDER BY sequence, which rows does this average cover?
options: Every row in the partition, since ROWS BETWEEN only affects processing order, not which rows are included in the average.
Only the 3rd, 4th, and 5th rows -- the current row plus the two immediately preceding it in the ORDER BY sequence.
The 5th row together with the 6th and 7th rows that follow it.
All rows from the 1st through the 5th -- an expanding, running average.
assessments.explanation: `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` defines the frame as the current row plus the two rows immediately before it. For the 5th row, that's rows 3, 4, and 5. The “All rows from the 1st through…” option describes the behavior of the *default* frame when ORDER BY is present but no ROWS/RANGE clause is given. The “The 5th row together with the 6th…” option reverses the direction; PRECEDING means before the current row in the ordering, not after. The “Every row in the partition, since ROWS…” option misreads the frame clause as irrelevant to row inclusion, when its purpose is to define which rows are included.

concepts.title: Common Table Expressions and Recursive CTEs
concepts.description: A CTE names a subquery so a complex statement can be broken into readable, sequential steps; a recursive CTE extends the same WITH syntax to repeatedly apply a query to its own prior output, which is the standard way to traverse hierarchical or graph-shaped data in SQL.
learningObjectives: Write a CTE with WITH ... AS (...) and explain how it improves readability over deeply nested subqueries.
Chain multiple CTEs together, with a later CTE referencing an earlier one, to express a multi-step query as named, sequential stages.
Explain Postgres's CTE materialization behavior -- when a CTE is inlined into the outer query like a view versus computed once and reused -- and why it matters for performance.
Explain the two-part structure of a recursive CTE (a base case UNION ALL a recursive case) and trace how it executes iteratively.
Write a recursive CTE to traverse a hierarchical structure such as an org chart, and explain why a working termination condition is required.

sections.heading: WITH: Naming a Subquery for Readability
sections.body:
A **common table expression (CTE)**, introduced with `WITH name AS (subquery)`, gives a subquery a name that the rest of the statement can refer to as if it were an ordinary table. Nothing a CTE does is impossible with a plain nested subquery; the value is readability, especially once a query has more than one or two logical steps.

```sql
-- Nested subquery: readable only if you're comfortable reading inside-out
SELECT customer_id, order_count
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) AS customer_orders
WHERE order_count > 5;

-- The equivalent CTE: reads top-to-bottom, each step named
WITH customer_orders AS (
    SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, order_count
FROM customer_orders
WHERE order_count > 5;
```

Both queries produce identical results and, in this simple case, an identical execution plan. The naming pays off as a query grows: instead of parentheses nested three or four levels deep and read from the inside out, a chain of CTEs reads top to bottom.

sections.heading: Chaining Multiple CTEs
sections.body:
A `WITH` clause can define more than one CTE, separated by commas, and any CTE after the first can reference the ones defined before it, which turns a multi-stage computation into a readable pipeline. A CTE exists only for the one statement that defines it, and its name shadows any real table of the same name within that statement.

```sql
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_growth AS (
    SELECT month, revenue,
           revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS revenue_change
    FROM monthly_revenue
)
SELECT month, revenue, revenue_change
FROM monthly_growth
WHERE revenue_change < 0
ORDER BY month;
```

`monthly_revenue` computes one aggregate step; `monthly_growth`, referencing `monthly_revenue` by name, builds a window-function calculation on top of it; the final SELECT filters and orders the result of that second stage. To debug one stage, temporarily change the final SELECT to `SELECT * FROM monthly_revenue`.

sections.heading: Materialization: When a CTE Is (and Isn't) Optimized Like a Subquery
sections.body:
For a long time, Postgres always materialized a CTE: it ran the CTE as a separate step and stored the rows, so the planner could not push a filter from the outer query down *into* it as it can with an ordinary subquery. On a large table that could be a performance cliff, because an outer `WHERE id = 42` was applied only after the CTE had produced every row.

Postgres 12 changed this default: a non-recursive CTE that's referenced exactly once, and has no side effects (no data-modifying statement, no volatile functions), is **inlined** into the outer query, and the planner can push down predicates as if you'd nested the subquery. A CTE is still materialized if it's referenced more than once, if it's recursive, or if you write `AS MATERIALIZED`. For a CTE referenced twice, `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` asks for inlining anyway, which pays off when each reference has its own selective filter that can use an index. `EXPLAIN` shows which you got: a materialized CTE appears as a `CTE Scan` node.

Data-modifying CTEs follow different rules. `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` statements inside `WITH` run exactly once and to completion whether or not the outer query reads their output, and they are never inlined:

```sql
-- Archive old rows and delete them in one statement
WITH moved AS (
    DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_date < '2025-01-01'
    RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
```

So on Postgres 12+, don't assume a CTE is a performance boundary. Check `EXPLAIN` when it matters, and write `MATERIALIZED` when you want an expensive result computed once and reused instead of recomputed per reference.

sections.heading: Recursive CTEs: Base Case, Recursive Case, and How They Execute
sections.body:
A **recursive CTE**, declared with `WITH RECURSIVE`, is built from two parts joined by `UNION` or `UNION ALL`: a **base case** (an ordinary, non-recursive query that produces the starting rows) and a **recursive case** (a query that references the CTE's own name, building the next 'layer' of rows from the previous layer).

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    -- Base case: the top of the hierarchy (no manager)
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive case: each employee whose manager is already in org_chart
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM org_chart ORDER BY depth, name;
```

Execution proceeds iteratively, not all at once: Postgres first runs the base case, producing an initial working set (here, employees with no manager, depth 1). It then repeatedly runs the recursive case, each time joining `employees` against only the rows produced in the *previous* iteration (not the whole accumulated result so far), producing the next layer: depth 2 (direct reports of the top-level people), then depth 3 (their reports), and so on. Each iteration's output is added to the final result, and the whole process stops automatically the moment an iteration produces zero new rows. Despite the name, this is a loop over a work queue rather than a recursive function call. Prefer `UNION ALL`: plain `UNION` also removes duplicates at every step, which costs a sort or hash. The recursive term may refer to the CTE only once and not from inside a subquery; Postgres rejects anything else with an error.

sections.heading: Termination, Infinite Loops, and Cycle Detection
sections.body:
A recursive CTE terminates only when an iteration of the recursive case produces zero new rows to add. For a tree-shaped hierarchy this happens by itself: eventually you reach employees with no reports and the recursive case finds nothing to join. But suppose a data-entry mistake makes employee 5 report to 8, and 8 report to 5. The query above never notices, because neither has a NULL manager and so neither is reachable from the root; both just vanish from the chart. Start the traversal *inside* the cycle, with `WHERE id = 5`, and the recursive case alternates between 5 and 8 forever, depth increasing, until it fills the disk with temporary files, hits `statement_timeout`, or you cancel it. Switching to `UNION`, which discards duplicate rows, doesn't help here, because the growing depth makes every row different.

The defensive pattern is to track the path already visited and stop extending it if a row would revisit something already in it:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path
    FROM employees WHERE id = 5

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1, oc.path || e.id
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
    WHERE e.id <> ALL(oc.path)   -- refuse to revisit a node already in this path
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM org_chart ORDER BY depth, name;
```

`path` accumulates every id visited so far on this branch, and `WHERE e.id <> ALL(oc.path)` refuses to extend the branch back into one of them. Postgres 14 added built-in syntax for this, `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path` appended after the recursive query, which keeps the path array for you. It emits the repeated row once with `is_cycle = true`, so add `WHERE NOT is_cycle` to the outer query if you don't want it. Use one or the other whenever the data *might* contain cycles, including graphs such as follows or package dependencies where cycles are normal.

examples.title: Refactoring a Nested Subquery Into a Readable CTE
examples.code:
-- Nested version: reads inside-out, hard to skim
SELECT product_id, avg_rating
FROM (
    SELECT product_id, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating
    FROM reviews
    GROUP BY product_id
) AS product_ratings
WHERE avg_rating >= 4.0
ORDER BY avg_rating DESC;

-- CTE version: reads top-to-bottom, each stage named
WITH product_ratings AS (
    SELECT product_id, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating
    FROM reviews
    GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT product_id, avg_rating
FROM product_ratings
WHERE avg_rating >= 4.0
ORDER BY avg_rating DESC;
examples.explanation: On Postgres 12+ both produce the same plan, since a single-reference, non-recursive CTE is inlined. What changes is reading order: in the nested version you have to find the innermost parentheses before the outer WHERE makes sense. The CTE version names the intermediate result first, so the final SELECT reads as a next step instead of a puzzle to unpack. With the filter on an aggregate, the planner can't push `avg_rating >= 4.0` below the GROUP BY in either form; it becomes the equivalent of a HAVING clause.

examples.title: Recursive CTE: Traversing an Org Chart With Depth and Path
examples.code:
-- employees: (1, 'Amara', NULL), (2, 'Ben', 1), (3, 'Cara', 1), (4, 'Dan', 2)

WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth, name::text AS path
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1, oc.path || ' > ' || e.name
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT name, depth, path FROM org_chart ORDER BY depth, name;

-- name  | depth | path
-- Amara |   1   | Amara
-- Ben   |   2   | Amara > Ben
-- Cara  |   2   | Amara > Cara
-- Dan   |   3   | Amara > Ben > Dan
examples.explanation: The base case selects only Amara, the one employee with `manager_id IS NULL`, at depth 1, with a path containing her own name. The recursive case then runs repeatedly: its first execution joins `employees` against the base case's output (just Amara), finding Ben and Cara (both report to Amara, id 1), producing depth 2 rows with paths extended from Amara's. Its second execution joins `employees` against *that* layer (Ben and Cara), finding Dan (who reports to Ben, id 2), producing a depth-3 row. Its third execution finds no employee reporting to anyone in the previous layer, produces zero new rows, and the recursion stops there. The `path` column is built up at each layer so the final result shows the chain of managers above each employee. Ordering by `path` instead of `depth` would list each person under their manager, ready to render as a tree. The `::text` cast in the base case is there because a recursive CTE requires the two halves' column types to match, and `||` produces text: without it, a `varchar` name column fails with a type mismatch error.

examples.title: Chained CTEs: Monthly Revenue, Then Month-Over-Month Change
examples.code:
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_growth AS (
    SELECT month, revenue,
           revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS revenue_change
    FROM monthly_revenue
)
SELECT month, revenue, revenue_change
FROM monthly_growth
WHERE revenue_change < 0
ORDER BY month;
examples.explanation: `monthly_revenue` reduces raw order rows down to one row per month with a summed total. `monthly_growth`, defined second, references `monthly_revenue` by name as if it were a table, and applies a window function (`LAG`, which looks at the previous row in an ordering) to compute how much each month's revenue changed from the prior month. The final SELECT then filters down to only the months where revenue dropped. The first month has no predecessor, so its `revenue_change` is NULL and the filter drops it. A month with no orders has no row at all, and LAG then compares against the last month that does; join to `generate_series` if gaps are possible.

misconceptions.description: A CTE is always fully computed once and reused, unlike a subquery, which is always more heavily optimized by the planner -- so CTEs are inherently slower than the equivalent subquery.
misconceptions.clarification: This was true of every Postgres version before 12, where a CTE was always materialized as a separate step the planner couldn't optimize across. Postgres 12 changed the default: a non-recursive CTE referenced exactly once, with no side effects, is inlined into the outer query just as an ordinary subquery would be, predicate pushdown included. A CTE is still materialized if it's referenced more than once, if it's recursive, or if `AS MATERIALIZED` is specified. On modern Postgres the answer depends on how the CTE is used and which version you run, not on a blanket rule that CTEs are a performance wall.

misconceptions.description: A recursive CTE will safely traverse any hierarchical-looking data, because SQL detects and prevents infinite loops caused by cycles automatically.
misconceptions.clarification: There is no automatic cycle detection in a standard recursive CTE. If the traversal reaches a cycle (employee A transitively reports to themselves, for instance) and the recursive case doesn't guard against revisiting a node, the query loops until a resource limit is hit or it is canceled. Safe traversal of data that might contain cycles requires either manually tracking the path visited so far and refusing to extend into an already-visited node (`WHERE e.id <> ALL(oc.path)`), or, from Postgres 14 onward, the built-in `CYCLE ... SET ... USING ...` clause, which does the same bookkeeping. Either way you have to ask for it.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this deeply nested subquery, which finds departments where the average salary exceeds $80,000 along with each department's headcount, as a chain of two readable CTEs.
exercises.code:
SELECT department, avg_salary, headcount
FROM (
    SELECT d.department,
           (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.department = d.department) AS avg_salary,
           (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.department = d.department) AS headcount
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees) d
) dept_stats
WHERE avg_salary > 80000;
hints: The first logical step is: for each department, compute the average salary and headcount in one pass. That's a GROUP BY, not the correlated per-department subqueries the original uses.
Name that first step as a CTE, then filter on it in a second CTE that the final SELECT reads from.
You don't need two separate correlated subqueries for avg_salary and headcount: GROUP BY with AVG() and COUNT() in the same query computes both together, once per department.
exercises.solutionCode:
WITH dept_stats AS (
    SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary, COUNT(*) AS headcount
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY department
),
high_paying AS (
    SELECT department, avg_salary, headcount
    FROM dept_stats
    WHERE avg_salary > 80000
)
SELECT department, avg_salary, headcount
FROM high_paying;
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original query recomputes AVG and COUNT via two separate correlated subqueries per department: for each row of the distinct-department list, it re-scans `employees` twice, filtering to that one department each time. The CTE version replaces all of that with a single GROUP BY that computes both aggregates for every department in one pass, then names that result `dept_stats` so `high_paying` can filter on `avg_salary`. It is also usually faster, since it scans `employees` once instead of repeatedly per department. For this particular question the second CTE is optional: `HAVING AVG(salary) > 80000` on the first one does the same filtering. Two stages are shown because the exercise is about chaining. One difference to know about: rows with a NULL department form a group in the GROUP BY version, whereas in the original `e.department = d.department` is never TRUE for NULL, so that group's average comes out NULL and is filtered away. Add `WHERE department IS NOT NULL` if the column is nullable.

exercises.prompt: This recursive CTE is meant to list employee 5 and everyone under them, but on this dataset it runs forever and never returns. The employees table has a bad row: employee 5 lists employee 8 as their manager, and employee 8 lists employee 5 as their manager (a cyclic data-entry error). Fix the query so it terminates safely even with this bad data.
exercises.code:
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE id = 5

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM reports ORDER BY depth;
hints: Employee 5 reports to 8, and employee 8 reports to 5. Once both are in the recursive result, each iteration will keep rediscovering the other one as a 'new' row forever.
Track the chain of ids visited so far on each branch of the traversal, and refuse to extend a branch back into a node that's already in that chain.

An array column (built with ARRAY[...] in the base case and || in the recursive case) combined with a WHERE clause checking `<> ALL(...)` is the standard hand-rolled fix; Postgres 14+ also offers a built-in CYCLE clause.
exercises.solutionCode:
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path
    FROM employees
    WHERE id = 5

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1, r.path || e.id
    FROM employees e
    JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
    WHERE e.id <> ALL(r.path)
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM reports ORDER BY depth;
exercises.solutionExplanation: The base case yields 5 at depth 1. The next iteration finds 8 (its manager is 5), the next finds 5 again (its manager is 8), and so on with depth increasing without bound. With `path` accumulating every id visited on the branch, the step from 8 back to 5 is rejected by `WHERE e.id <> ALL(r.path)` because 5 is already in `{5,8}`, so the cycle contributes 5 and 8 once each and the recursion ends when the remaining branches are explored. The check is per branch, not global: two different branches can still reach the same node (a diamond in a reporting structure), and each path is listed separately, which is usually what an org-chart query wants.

assessments.prompt: A recursive CTE traverses a category tree and is expected to terminate once it reaches the leaf categories (those with no subcategories). What causes a recursive CTE's execution to stop?
options: It stops the moment an iteration of the recursive case produces zero new rows to add to the result.
It always stops automatically after exactly 100 iterations, as a built-in Postgres safety limit.
It stops as soon as the base case has run once, since the recursive case only runs a single additional time by definition.
It stops only when an explicit LIMIT clause is reached in the final SELECT.
assessments.explanation: A recursive CTE executes its recursive case repeatedly, each time operating only on the rows produced by the previous iteration, and stops as soon as an iteration contributes zero new rows. The “It always stops automatically after exactly 100…” option invents a fixed iteration cap that doesn't exist by default (SQL Server does default to MAXRECURSION 100; Postgres has no such limit, which is why an unguarded cyclic traversal can run forever). The “It stops as soon as the base…” option misunderstands the mechanism: the recursive case runs however many times are needed, layer by layer, not just once. The “It stops only when an explicit LIMIT…” option is wrong because the recursion needs no LIMIT to end. Postgres may stop evaluating early once the outer query has fetched enough rows, but the documentation warns against relying on that, and adding ORDER BY or a join defeats it.

assessments.prompt: Explain how a recursive CTE executes, step by step, using the base case and recursive case, and explain why a recursive CTE over data that might contain cycles needs an explicit safeguard rather than relying on SQL to detect the cycle automatically.
assessments.modelAnswer: A recursive CTE is built from two parts combined with UNION or UNION ALL: a base case, which is an ordinary query producing the starting set of rows, and a recursive case, which references the CTE's own name and describes how to derive the next layer of rows from the previous layer. Execution is iterative rather than a single pass: Postgres runs the base case once to produce an initial working set, then repeatedly runs the recursive case, each time joining against only the rows that the *immediately preceding* iteration produced, not the whole accumulated result. Each iteration's output is appended to the final result and also becomes the input to the next iteration. This continues layer by layer (for a hierarchy: depth 1, depth 2, depth 3, and so on) until some iteration produces zero new rows, at which point the accumulated result is returned. If the traversal enters a cycle, that condition is never reached: node A leads back to node A, the recursive case has no way of recognizing 'I've already visited this node on this branch,' and it rediscovers the same nodes forever, consuming more memory and time with each pass. A plain WITH RECURSIVE ... UNION ALL has no notion of 'don't revisit a node.' (UNION discards rows identical to earlier ones, but a depth or path column makes each revisit look different.) The fix is to carry the path of visited nodes as an array in each row, and add a condition to the recursive case's WHERE clause that refuses to extend a branch into any node already in its path. Postgres 14's CYCLE clause performs this bookkeeping, but it too has to be written into the query. Only cycles reachable from the base case's rows matter; a cycle elsewhere in the table is never visited.

assessments.prompt: On Postgres 12+, under which of these conditions is a non-recursive CTE still forced to materialize (computed once, held separately) rather than being inlined into the outer query like an ordinary subquery?
options: Whenever the CTE's name is alphabetically later than the names of the tables it queries.
CTEs are never materialized on Postgres 12+ -- automatic materialization was removed entirely in that version.
Whenever the CTE's own query includes a WHERE clause.
Whenever the CTE is referenced more than once in the outer query, or is explicitly marked AS MATERIALIZED.
assessments.explanation: A non-recursive CTE referenced exactly once, with no side effects, is inlined by default on Postgres 12+; referencing it more than once or writing AS MATERIALIZED causes it to be computed once and held separately. The “Whenever the CTE's own query includes a WHERE clause” option invents an irrelevant condition. The “Whenever the CTE's name is alphabetically later…” option has no basis in how the planner works. The “CTEs are never materialized on Postgres 12+…” option overstates the change: materialization stopped being the default for the single-reference case, but recursive and multiply-referenced CTEs are still materialized.

assessments.prompt: A recursive CTE's base case, due to a data problem, returns zero rows for a particular run (for instance, a corrupted org chart where every employee has some manager_id set, so `WHERE manager_id IS NULL` matches nobody). What happens?
options: Postgres substitutes the full table as a fallback base case whenever the declared base case returns nothing.
Postgres raises a runtime error, because a recursive CTE requires its base case to return at least one row to be valid.
The recursive case has no rows from a preceding iteration to join against.
The recursive case still runs once anyway, using the entire underlying table as an implicit starting point.
assessments.explanation: The recursive case joins against the previous iteration's output. If the base case produces zero rows, there is nothing to join against, so the CTE ends immediately with an empty result: the usual termination condition, met on the first iteration. A common real cause is a root row that points at itself (its `manager_id` equals its own `id`) instead of holding NULL, so the base case finds nobody; the fix belongs in the base-case condition, not in the recursion. The “The recursive case still runs once anyway…” and “Postgres substitutes the full table…” options both invent fallback behaviors that don't exist. The “Postgres raises a runtime error…” option is wrong; an empty base case is valid SQL and produces an empty result.

assessments.prompt: A CTE named `expensive_calc` performs a costly aggregation and is referenced twice within the outer query's SELECT list. On Postgres 12+, how many times is the aggregation computed by default?
options: Twice -- once for each reference, exactly as if the subquery had been pasted inline at both locations.

Once -- because it's referenced more than once, Postgres forces the CTE to materialize, computing it a single time and reusing the stored result for both references, unless AS NOT MATERIALIZED is explicitly specified to force separate re-evaluation.
The number of computations depends only on how many rows expensive_calc returns, not on how many times it's referenced in the outer query.
Zero times until the final result is actually fetched by the client, at which point it's computed lazily for whichever reference is read first.
assessments.explanation: Being referenced more than once causes a CTE to be materialized even on Postgres 12+: it's computed once and the stored result is reused. The “Twice -- once for each reference, exactly…” option describes what AS NOT MATERIALIZED would do, which helps when each reference filters down to a few rows. The “Zero times until the final result…” option is wrong about the count: Postgres does produce a CTE's rows on demand, but both references need them, and the stored rows are shared. The “The number of computations depends only…” option confuses row count with reference count, and only the latter affects materialization.

concepts.title: Correlated vs Uncorrelated Subqueries
concepts.description: An uncorrelated subquery is evaluated once, independently of the outer query; a correlated subquery references a column from the outer query and conceptually depends on each outer row, which changes how you reason about its result, its performance, and when EXISTS is the more idiomatic and safer choice than IN.
learningObjectives: Distinguish correlated from uncorrelated subqueries by checking whether the subquery references a column from its enclosing query.
Use an uncorrelated subquery in WHERE (with IN, =, or ANY), in FROM as a derived table, and in the SELECT list as a scalar subquery.
Use a correlated subquery with EXISTS or NOT EXISTS to test a relationship across tables without risking duplicate output rows.

Explain how Postgres's planner can execute a correlated subquery as a semi-join or anti-join internally, rather than literally re-running it once per outer row, and why indexing the correlated column still matters.
Rewrite a correlated subquery as an equivalent JOIN or window function where appropriate, and explain the trade-offs between the two forms.

sections.heading: Uncorrelated Subqueries: Evaluated Independently of the Outer Query
sections.body:
A subquery is **uncorrelated** when it doesn't reference any column from the query it's embedded in. You could paste it into psql and run it on its own.

```sql
-- Uncorrelated: this subquery's result doesn't depend on any outer row
SELECT name, total_spent
FROM customers
WHERE total_spent > (SELECT AVG(total_spent) FROM customers);
```

The subquery `(SELECT AVG(total_spent) FROM customers)` computes one number, the overall average, which is the same whichever `customers` row is being checked. Postgres evaluates it once and reuses the value for every comparison. Uncorrelated subqueries also show up as **derived tables** in a `FROM` clause (`FROM (SELECT ...) AS alias`, functionally similar to a CTE) and as **scalar subqueries** in a SELECT list. A scalar subquery returns one column; if it returns two rows at run time the query fails with 'more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression'. If it returns zero rows, the result is NULL rather than an error. In `SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE orders.customer_id = customers.id) FROM customers`, the subquery *does* reference an outer column, `customers.id`, so it is correlated. Position (WHERE, FROM, or SELECT) doesn't decide that; referencing an outer column does.

sections.heading: Correlated Subqueries: A Subquery That Depends on Each Outer Row
sections.body:
A subquery is **correlated** when it references a column from its enclosing query, so its result can differ for each outer row. For example, finding employees who earn more than their own department's average:

```sql
SELECT e.name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.department = e.department   -- references the OUTER row's department
);
```

The inner `SELECT AVG(e2.salary) ... WHERE e2.department = e.department` can't run on its own, because `e.department` belongs to the outer query. It reads as 'for each employee, compute their department's average salary, then compare.' The inner alias `e2` is what makes this work. Write `WHERE department = department` and both names resolve to the inner table, so the condition is true for every row and you get the company-wide average instead.

sections.heading: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS: The Idiomatic Correlated Pattern
sections.body:
The most common, idiomatic use of a correlated subquery is testing whether a matching row exists, with `EXISTS` or `NOT EXISTS`. Recall the NOT IN / NULL trap: one NULL in the subquery's result means `NOT IN` is never TRUE, and the query returns zero rows. `NOT EXISTS` doesn't have that problem. To see it, suppose one `order_items` row has a NULL `product_id`:

```sql
-- returns zero rows, even for products that were never ordered
SELECT name FROM products
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items);

-- returns the never-ordered products
SELECT name FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id);
```

`id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` expands to `id <> 1 AND id <> 2 AND id <> NULL`. The last comparison is UNKNOWN for every id, so the whole condition can never be TRUE.

```sql
-- Authors who have published at least one post
SELECT a.name
FROM authors a
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM posts p WHERE p.author_id = a.id
);
```

`EXISTS` doesn't care what columns the subquery selects -- `SELECT 1` is idiomatic because the column values are irrelevant, and Postgres can stop searching at the first match. This is also the safe alternative to an INNER JOIN when the only goal is an existence check: joining `authors` to `posts` on `author_id` would produce one row *per matching post* (an author with three posts appears three times), whereas `EXISTS` asks a yes/no question about each author and so returns each at most once.

sections.heading: Performance: How Postgres Executes a Correlated Subquery
sections.body:
'Runs once per outer row' describes what a correlated subquery *means*, and whether Postgres *executes* it that way depends on the shape. `EXISTS` and `IN (SELECT ...)` in WHERE are usually turned into a **semi-join**, and `NOT EXISTS` into an **anti-join**: one join operation that can hash or merge both inputs. `NOT IN` is not given the same treatment, because its NULL semantics differ from an anti-join's; it typically appears as a hashed subplan, or a much slower plain one if the hash wouldn't fit in `work_mem`. And a correlated *scalar* subquery, such as the department average above, isn't converted to a join at all. It shows up in `EXPLAIN` as a `SubPlan`, executed for each outer row.

Indexing matters differently in each case. For a semi- or anti-join, an index on `posts.author_id` lets Postgres probe for just the authors it needs; without one it reads all of `posts` once and hashes it, which is fine when you're checking most authors and wasteful when you're checking ten. For a SubPlan the index is critical, because without it every outer row triggers another full scan of the inner table. Check `EXPLAIN` on any table of meaningful size, and look at the `loops=` count in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.

sections.heading: When to Rewrite as a JOIN or a Window Function Instead
sections.body:
A correlated subquery computing a per-row aggregate, like the 'earns more than their department's average' example, can often be rewritten with a window function, `AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY department)`, which computes each department's average once instead of once per employee:

```sql
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, department, salary,
           AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
    FROM employees
) e
WHERE salary > dept_avg;
```

The window version sorts the table once, so it scales better as employees per department grow. The correlated version can still win when the outer query has already narrowed down to a handful of employees and `department` is indexed. `EXISTS`/`NOT EXISTS` generally should **not** be rewritten as a plain JOIN for an existence check, because of the duplicate-row risk. Collapsing the JOIN's output again with DISTINCT is more work, and easy to get wrong: `SELECT DISTINCT a.name` also merges two different authors who share a name. Between the two forms of the aggregate comparison, the choice often comes down to readability and what you can measure, so run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on realistic data instead of assuming either wins.

examples.title: Uncorrelated Subquery: Customers Above the Overall Average
examples.code:
SELECT name, total_spent
FROM customers
WHERE total_spent > (SELECT AVG(total_spent) FROM customers);

-- The subquery's plan runs ONCE, producing a single number,
-- which is then reused for every row's comparison.
-- (Simplified; PostgreSQL 17+ prints "(InitPlan 1).col1" instead of $0.)
EXPLAIN SELECT name, total_spent
FROM customers
WHERE total_spent > (SELECT AVG(total_spent) FROM customers);
-- Seq Scan on customers
--   Filter: (total_spent > $0)
--   InitPlan 1 (returns $0)
--     -> Aggregate
--          -> Seq Scan on customers customers_1
examples.explanation: The `EXPLAIN` output shows the subquery as an `InitPlan`, computed once, producing a value (`$0`) that the outer scan's filter reuses for every row. That is possible only because the subquery references nothing about the row being checked: `AVG(total_spent)` over the whole table means the same thing whichever row the filter is looking at, and `$0` is the placeholder the plan uses for that single value. A correlated scalar subquery would appear as a `SubPlan` instead.

examples.title: Correlated Subquery: Employees Above Their Own Department's Average
examples.code:
SELECT e.name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.department = e.department
);

-- Equivalent rewrite using a window function instead:
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, department, salary,
           AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
    FROM employees
) e
WHERE salary > dept_avg;
examples.explanation: The correlated version's inner subquery references `e.department`, so Postgres runs it as a SubPlan for every employee, recomputing the same department's average for each colleague. The window-function rewrite computes each average once, and the outer WHERE compares salary with the `dept_avg` column on the same row. The results match as long as `department` is never NULL: the correlated version drops such employees (`NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN), while PARTITION BY puts them together in one partition. Postgres may also execute the correlated form acceptably on a small table, so measure with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on realistic data before rewriting.

examples.title: EXISTS Avoids the Duplicate-Row Risk of a Plain JOIN
examples.code:
-- authors: (1, 'Amara'), (2, 'Ben' -- has zero posts)
-- posts: (1, 'SQL Basics', author_id=1), (2, 'Advanced SQL', author_id=1)

-- JOIN approach: Amara appears TWICE, once per matching post
SELECT a.name FROM authors a
JOIN posts p ON p.author_id = a.id;
-- Amara
-- Amara

-- EXISTS approach: Amara appears ONCE, regardless of post count
SELECT a.name FROM authors a
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM posts p WHERE p.author_id = a.id);
-- Amara
examples.explanation: The JOIN produces one output row per matching pair, so an author with two posts contributes two rows: correct if you wanted post-level detail, wrong if the goal was 'list authors who have published something.' EXISTS asks 'does at least one post exist with this author_id' for each author, and Postgres can stop at the first match. The duplicates are easy to miss in development, where most test authors have one post, and then inflate a `COUNT(*)` in production.

misconceptions.description: A correlated subquery always executes literally once per outer row, in a naive nested loop, no matter what -- so correlated subqueries are inherently slow and should be avoided.
misconceptions.clarification: That's a useful mental model for understanding what a correlated subquery *means*, but not always how Postgres *executes* one. The planner usually turns EXISTS into a semi-join and NOT EXISTS into an anti-join, executed as a single join. Correlated scalar subqueries (and NOT IN) don't get that rewrite, so a SubPlan over an unindexed column can be as slow as feared. Whether the correlated column is indexed usually matters more than correlation itself. Check EXPLAIN to see which one you have.

misconceptions.description: Any correlated subquery using EXISTS could just as easily be written as a plain JOIN with no real difference in behavior.
misconceptions.clarification: A JOIN and an EXISTS-based correlated subquery answer different questions. A JOIN produces one output row for every matching pair across the two tables, so a row with several matches is repeated once per match. EXISTS asks a yes/no question per outer row and can never return that row more than once. Converting an EXISTS check into a JOIN can introduce duplicate rows that someone then has to remember to remove. Use a JOIN when you want the matching rows themselves, and EXISTS when you only need to know that one exists.

exercises.prompt: Write a query that lists every product that has never appeared in any order, using a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery rather than NOT IN (to avoid the NULL trap covered in an earlier module).
exercises.code:
-- Tables: products(id, name), order_items(product_id, order_id)
-- Write a query using NOT EXISTS to find products with zero order_items rows.
hints: The subquery needs to reference the outer product's id to check whether THAT product has any matching order_items row, which makes it correlated.
NOT EXISTS asks 'does no matching row exist'. It doesn't matter what columns the inner SELECT returns, only whether any row satisfies the correlation condition.
Contrast this with NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items), which would be vulnerable to returning zero rows if order_items.product_id ever contains a NULL.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The subquery `SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id` is correlated because it references `p.id` from the outer query: for each product, it checks whether any order_items row references that product. NOT EXISTS keeps the products for which none was found. Unlike `NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items)`, a NULL product_id has no effect, since it never equals any `p.id`. The `1` in `SELECT 1` is arbitrary; `SELECT *` would behave the same. Postgres also plans this as an anti-join, which it can't do for NOT IN.

exercises.prompt: This query is meant to list each customer exactly once if they've placed at least one order over $500, but it returns some customers multiple times. Find the bug and fix it using EXISTS instead.
exercises.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.amount > 500;
hints: A JOIN produces one row per matching pair. If a customer has THREE orders over $500, how many times does that customer's row appear in this result?
The actual requirement described is an existence check ('has at least one'), not a request for every matching order row.
Rewrite it as a correlated subquery with EXISTS, checking per customer whether any of their orders exceeds 500, rather than joining and then having to deduplicate afterward.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original JOIN produces one result row for every matching (customer, order) pair where the order exceeds $500, so a customer with three qualifying orders appears three times. The EXISTS version asks, per customer, whether at least one order with amount > 500 exists, so each qualifying customer appears exactly once. Patching the JOIN with `SELECT DISTINCT c.name` would hide the repeats but also merge different customers who happen to share a name.

assessments.prompt:
Which of these two subqueries is correlated, and why?
```sql
-- Query A
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);

-- Query B
SELECT * FROM products p WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category);
```
options: Both queries are correlated, because both subqueries appear inside a WHERE clause comparing against price.
Both queries are uncorrelated, because both subqueries independently compute an AVG(price) value.

Query B is correlated, because its subquery references p.category from the outer query, making its result depend on which outer row is being evaluated; Query A's subquery references nothing from the outer query, so it's uncorrelated and evaluated only once.
Query A is correlated, because it appears in a WHERE clause; Query B is uncorrelated, because it uses a different table alias (p2) than the outer query.
assessments.explanation: Correlation depends on whether the subquery references a column from its enclosing query, not on which clause it appears in or what alias it uses. Query A's subquery references nothing outside itself, so it yields one number that can be computed once. Query B's subquery references `p.category` from the outer row, so its result changes with the product being checked. The “Query A is correlated, because it appears…”, “Both queries are correlated, because both subqueries…”, and “Both queries are uncorrelated, because both subqueries…” options all use a different test (clause, aggregate, or alias).

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between a correlated and an uncorrelated subquery, and explain why EXISTS is generally preferred over a plain JOIN when the goal is checking whether a related row exists, rather than retrieving the related rows.
assessments.modelAnswer: The distinguishing test between a correlated and an uncorrelated subquery is whether the subquery references any column from the query it's embedded in. An uncorrelated subquery doesn't, and could be run on its own, so Postgres can evaluate an uncorrelated subquery once and reuse its result across every row of the outer query, which is why something like `WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)` only computes that average a single time. A correlated subquery, by contrast, references a column belonging to the outer query (such as `WHERE p2.category = p.category`, where `p.category` comes from the outer row), so its result depends on which outer row is being evaluated. Postgres turns correlated EXISTS and NOT EXISTS into semi-joins and anti-joins; a correlated scalar subquery runs as a SubPlan for each row. So correlation describes what the query means, while its cost depends on the plan, which you check with EXPLAIN. EXISTS is generally better than a JOIN for existence checks because the two answer different questions. A JOIN produces one output row for every matching pair, so a row with several matches is repeated, which is right when you want that detail and wrong when the question is 'does at least one match exist.' EXISTS evaluates to true or false per outer row, and Postgres can stop searching at the first match. That avoids the duplicates, avoids a DISTINCT to clean them up (which could also merge distinct rows that look alike), and states the intent plainly.

assessments.prompt: `SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE orders.customer_id = customers.id) FROM customers` places a subquery directly in the SELECT list. Is this subquery correlated or uncorrelated, and why?
options: Correlated, because it references customers.id, a column belonging to the outer query.
Uncorrelated, because scalar subqueries placed in the SELECT list are always evaluated exactly once regardless of their content.
Uncorrelated, because COUNT(*) is an aggregate function, and aggregate functions can never appear inside a correlated subquery.
It cannot be determined from the SQL text alone; correlation is a runtime property only visible by running EXPLAIN.
assessments.explanation: `orders.customer_id = customers.id` references `customers.id`, an outer-query column, so the subquery's result depends on which customer row is being evaluated: it's correlated. The “Uncorrelated, because scalar subqueries placed…” option wrongly assumes clause position determines correlation; a scalar subquery in the SELECT list can be either correlated or uncorrelated depending on its content. The “Uncorrelated, because COUNT(*) is an aggregate function…” option is false; the department-average query uses AVG in a correlated subquery. The “It cannot be determined from the SQL…” option is wrong; correlation is visible in the SQL text.

assessments.prompt: A correlated `NOT EXISTS` subquery filters on `p.author_id = a.id`, and `posts.author_id` has no index at all, on a `posts` table with many rows. What's the most accurate expectation for its performance?
options: Performance is unaffected either way, since NOT EXISTS is always rewritten into an anti-join that ignores indexes entirely.

The planner will usually choose an anti-join that reads and hashes all of posts once, which is acceptable when checking most authors but wasteful when checking only a few; an index on author_id lets it probe for just the authors it needs, and protects query shapes that end up probing posts once per outer row.
Only IN and EXISTS depend on indexing; NOT EXISTS specifically never benefits from an index under any circumstance.
NOT EXISTS is immune to missing indexes, because it always stops at the first matching row found regardless of how that row is located.
assessments.explanation: NOT EXISTS becomes an anti-join. With no index, Postgres has to read the whole posts table at least once to build a hash (or sort it). With an index it can also use a nested-loop or merge anti-join that touches only the relevant entries, so the cost follows the number of authors checked instead of the size of posts. The “Performance is unaffected either way, since NOT…” and “Only IN and EXISTS depend on indexing…” options both wrongly claim indexes are irrelevant, but an anti-join can use an index like any other join. The “NOT EXISTS is immune to missing indexes…” option is wrong because stopping at the first match doesn't help if finding it requires scanning many rows, and an author with no posts has no first match to stop at.

assessments.prompt: Someone proposes replacing `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.amount > 500)` with a `JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.amount > 500` followed by `SELECT DISTINCT c.name`. Would this produce the same final set of names, and is it a good idea?
options: No -- DISTINCT can only be applied to numeric columns, not text columns such as name, so this rewritten query would fail to run at all.
No -- the JOIN-plus-DISTINCT version can never produce the same set of customer names as the EXISTS version, regardless of the underlying data.
Yes, and it's strictly more efficient, because DISTINCT is applied before the JOIN executes, which reduces how many rows the JOIN has to scan.
Yes, it would produce the same final set of names, but it does strictly more work than necessary.
assessments.explanation: After deduplication, the JOIN-plus-DISTINCT version yields the same set of names, but it generates one row per matching order and then collapses them, whereas EXISTS needs at most one matching order per customer. The row counts can still differ: two customers with the same name are two rows from EXISTS and one after DISTINCT. The “No -- the JOIN-plus-DISTINCT version can never…” option is wrong because both queries select the customers with a qualifying order. The “Yes, and it's strictly more efficient…” option is backwards; DISTINCT operates on the JOIN's output, not before it, so it cannot reduce the JOIN's own scanning work. The “No -- DISTINCT can only be applied…” option is fabricated; DISTINCT works on text.
